## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kosiyajātaka* (Ja 130) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection, serving as the tenth and final story of the *Kusanāḷivagga* in the *Ekakanipāta* [Fausböll 1877]. The framing narrative is set at Jetavana concerning a woman of Sāvatthī, the deceitful wife of a devout and virtuous brahmin lay-follower; she was in the habit of roving about at night while feigning illness during the day to shirk household chores [SuttaCentral]. In modern scholarship on the social attitudes of Buddhist narrative literature, the story is cited as an example of a recurring motif where brāhmaṇa wives are depicted as unchaste or corrupt [Goyal 2003].
In the conclusion to the story, the brahmin woman ceases her improper conduct out of reverence for the Buddha; the Master then connects the birth (*jātakaṁ samodhānesi*), declaring that the husband and wife were the same couple in their previous existence, while the Buddha himself was their wise teacher (*ācariyo*) [Fausböll 1877].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists four translations of the Jātaka in four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
